sessions.title: UI foundations and the purpose of automation
sessions.summary: This session introduced the Academy learning routine and connected browser structure to UI test automation. The instructor demonstrated how HTML and CSS shape a page, why repeatable checks benefit from automation, and why testers must understand and verify AI-assisted test code.
keyConcepts: Timeouts and review of generated code

sections.title: HTML and inspection
sections.text: HTML describes the elements and structure of a web page. Browser inspection helps connect a visible control to the element that a test must find and interact with; understanding the structure comes before writing a reliable automation script.

sections.title: CSS and presentation
sections.text: CSS controls presentation such as layout, size and styling. The session compared different practice-site domains to show that a similar user task can have different visual designs. Test the required behavior as well as the visible interface.

sections.title: Why automate repeatable checks
sections.text: The discussion framed automation as a way to repeat checks efficiently and expand coverage. Automation still needs meaningful scenarios, expected outcomes, test data and a tester who investigates failures; it does not remove responsibility for quality.

sections.title: Timeouts and review of generated code
sections.text: The instructor emphasized understanding timeouts and parameterization even when AI helps write tests. A generated script must be reviewed and run against the intended application; receiving code is not evidence that the check works.

practice: Inspect one practice-page button and explain its purpose and markup.
Describe a repeatable user journey and its expected outcome before writing code.
Review generated test code and identify what each action and assertion is intended to prove.

terms.definition: HTML: the markup that describes page elements and structure.
CSS: rules that control page presentation.
Automation: executable checks that can be repeated consistently.

terms.term: Timeouts and review of generated code
terms.definition: Timeout: the allowed waiting period before an operation is reported as unsuccessful.

review.question: Why inspect the page before automating it?
review.answer: Inspection helps identify the real element and the attributes a test can use to locate it.

review.question: What is the difference between HTML and CSS?
review.answer: HTML describes structure and elements; CSS controls how they are presented.

review.question: Does automation eliminate the tester’s role?
review.answer: No. Testers choose scenarios, check outcomes and investigate failures.

review.question: Why review AI-generated tests?
review.answer: Generated code may select the wrong element, use unsuitable data or assert the wrong outcome.

review.question: What should you investigate after a timeout?
review.answer: Check the application state, the target element and the waiting condition before changing the timeout.

sessions.title: Course foundations, AI assistance and the testing journey
sessions.summary: This supplied session connects SDLC concepts and testability to the planned hands-on automation course. It introduces the distinction between UI and API checks, AI-assisted authoring, and the runtime needed to execute test scripts. Hosting and future-tool promises in the recording describe plans at the time, not current service availability.

sections.title: SDLC and testability
sections.text: Requirements should be understood and testable before execution begins. The discussion connected requirement review, design, development and testing so learners can explain where a check fits within the wider software lifecycle.

sections.title: API checks and request/response
sections.text: The course introduced API testing as a separate practice area alongside UI automation. A UI action may call an endpoint, but checking only the page does not by itself verify all request, response or data behavior.

sections.title: AI assistance and agents
sections.text: AI can assist with authoring repetitive test work, while tools and agents provide ways to act on a system. The tester must still supply context, verify the output and respect organizational data boundaries.

sections.title: Node and package execution
sections.text: The instructor discussed packaging test scripts and running them with Node and NPM. Reading a script or preparing code in an editor is distinct from executing it and collecting a test result.

practice: Map one requirement to a visible outcome and identify a related API check.
Explain the difference between an editor, a runtime and a test result.
Use approved practice data when discussing or generating examples.

terms.definition: Testability: how clearly a requirement can be checked through observable outcomes.
API testing: checking the behavior of an interface through requests and responses.
AI assistance: support for producing or explaining work that still requires review.
Runtime: the environment that actually executes a program.

review.question: Why does requirement review matter before test execution?
review.answer: It clarifies the intended behavior and whether it can be checked.

review.question: Are UI and API tests interchangeable?
review.answer: No. They observe different interfaces and may reveal different failures.

review.question: What context should accompany AI-assisted test authoring?
review.answer: The intended application behavior, scenario, allowed data and expected outcomes.

review.question: Does preparing code prove that a test passes?
review.answer: No. The code must execute against the intended environment and produce reviewed evidence.

review.question: What should a tester protect when using AI tools?
review.answer: Sensitive test data, organizational information and credentials.

sessions.title: SDLC, STLC and writing test cases
sessions.summary: This session introduced the tester’s place in the software lifecycle, the testing-specific activities within it, and the documents used to plan and execute checks. It also connected test cases to user stories and discussed how testing work is organized in an Agile team.

sections.title: Software development lifecycle
sections.text: SDLC describes the wider process of developing and maintaining software. In the class example, testers reviewed requirements, prepared checks, reported defects and supported later verification; the exact phase names and team responsibilities can vary by organization.

sections.title: Software testing lifecycle
sections.text: STLC organizes testing activities such as understanding requirements, planning, designing cases, executing checks and reporting results. Explain it as the testing work within the broader development lifecycle rather than a second unrelated project.

sections.title: Test planning
sections.text: A test plan describes the testing scope, approach, environment, responsibilities, risks and completion criteria. The session emphasized using the organization’s existing template and understanding the plan before executing tests.

sections.title: Test case evidence
sections.text: A test case connects an action or sequence of actions to an expected result. During execution, record the actual result and status so another person can understand what was checked and why it passed or failed.

sections.title: Sprints and team workflow
sections.text: The instructor used a two-week sprint example to explain iterative work and ceremonies. Treat that cadence as the class example rather than a universal release schedule; explain what the team does during planning, daily coordination, review and improvement.

practice: Describe one requirement and write an action, expected result and actual-result field.
Explain your testing contribution at each relevant lifecycle stage.
Practice a brief interview answer that connects planning, execution and reporting.

terms.definition: SDLC: the wider lifecycle of software development and maintenance.
STLC: the lifecycle of testing activities.
Test plan: an agreed description of how testing will be organized.
Test case: documented steps, expected results and execution evidence.
Sprint: a bounded period of iterative team work.

review.question: How do SDLC and STLC relate?
review.answer: SDLC covers the wider product lifecycle; STLC organizes the testing activities within it.

review.question: What does a test plan provide?
review.answer: Scope, approach, resources, risks and criteria that guide testing.

review.question: How do expected and actual results differ?
review.answer: Expected describes the intended outcome; actual records what happened during execution.

review.question: Why link a test case to a user story?
review.answer: The link shows which requirement the check covers.

review.question: Must every team use the sprint cadence shown in class?
review.answer: No. The cadence was an example and team arrangements may differ.

sessions.title: ServiceNow workflows and core QA interview concepts
sessions.summary: This session combined a ServiceNow demonstration with interview practice on verification, validation and defect reporting. It followed a requester action through backend workflow checks and emphasized role-based testing and clear test evidence.

sections.title: Role-based testing
sections.text: The demonstration used impersonation to check behavior as a designated test user. Verify the intended requester or fulfiller role in an approved test environment instead of assuming an administrator’s experience represents the user’s experience.

sections.title: ServiceNow workflow checks
sections.text: ServiceNow was used to demonstrate requests, incidents and problems. A useful end-to-end check follows the submitted request through its records and tasks, not just the success message shown on the portal.

sections.title: Verification and validation
sections.text: Verification examines requirements, documents and work products for correctness early in the process. Validation checks the implemented behavior against intended user needs; the session discussed how both contribute to finding and preventing problems.

sections.title: Severity and priority
sections.text: Severity describes the impact of an issue on functionality or users. Priority describes the urgency or order of fixing it. Keep the two fields distinct and explain the business context behind a proposed priority.

practice: Write a portal-to-backend test using approved requester and fulfiller roles.
Explain one verification activity and one validation activity.
Describe an issue’s impact separately from the urgency of fixing it.

terms.definition: Impersonation: testing a workflow using an authorized user role.
Workflow: the connected steps and state changes that fulfill a request.
Verification: checking work products; validation: checking intended product behavior.
Severity: impact. Priority: urgency of resolution.

review.question: Why test with a requester role?
review.answer: The requester’s permissions and experience may differ from an administrator’s.

review.question: Why inspect backend tasks after submission?
review.answer: They show whether the request progressed through the intended workflow.

review.question: How do verification and validation differ?
review.answer: Verification checks work products; validation checks implemented behavior against intended needs.

review.question: Can a low-severity issue have high priority?
review.answer: Yes, business timing or visibility can make its resolution urgent.

review.question: What belongs in a useful defect report?
review.answer: Clear steps, expected and actual behavior, evidence and the relevant environment.

sessions.title: Agile workflow and selecting useful test types
sessions.summary: This session revisited Agile coordination and then compared regression, smoke, negative, boundary and performance testing. The central interview skill is to explain why a particular check is appropriate and give a concrete example.

sections.title: Agile coordination
sections.text: The class reviewed story refinement, planning, stand-ups and review activities. Explain the purpose and your QA contribution rather than memorizing one team’s meeting calendar or assignment rules.

sections.title: Regression testing
sections.text: Regression checks look for unintended effects after a change. Select relevant existing behavior based on the affected features and risk; a defect fix should also be checked directly to confirm the original problem is resolved.

sections.title: Smoke testing
sections.text: Smoke testing provides a quick check that a build or application is stable enough for deeper testing. Opening the application is one example, but the selected smoke checks should cover the critical starting paths for the system.

sections.title: Positive and negative checks
sections.text: Positive checks use valid actions or data to confirm expected success. Negative checks use invalid or disallowed inputs and verify that the application handles them correctly instead of accepting them or failing unexpectedly.

sections.title: Boundary and performance checks
sections.text: Boundary testing focuses on the edges of permitted ranges. The session also introduced performance testing, where workload and response behavior matter; keep a boundary-value example separate from a performance scenario.

practice: For a form rule, propose valid, invalid and boundary cases.
Choose a small smoke set for a newly delivered build.
Explain how a changed feature could affect an existing workflow.

terms.definition: Agile coordination: iterative planning, feedback and team communication.
Regression: checking existing behavior after a change.
Smoke test: a small set of critical stability checks.
Negative testing: checking the handling of invalid or disallowed behavior.
Boundary: an edge of an allowed range. Performance: behavior under workload.

review.question: What is the purpose of regression testing?
review.answer: To detect unintended effects in existing behavior after a change.

review.question: How is confirming a fix different from regression?
review.answer: Confirmation checks the original defect; regression checks related existing behavior.

review.question: Why run smoke checks early?
review.answer: They can reveal a build that is not ready for detailed testing.

review.question: What should a negative test assert?
review.answer: The intended rejection or safe handling of invalid input.

review.question: Where should boundary values be selected?
review.answer: At the stated edges and just inside or outside the permitted range.

sessions.title: Agile interview answers and constructive retrospectives
sessions.summary: This coaching session reviewed how testers describe their Agile work, communicate test status and blockers, and suggest improvements. It also discussed identifying repetitive work that could benefit from automation.

sections.title: Daily test status
sections.text: Give a short, concrete update about completed testing, planned work and impediments. Useful status describes evidence and what is needed next, so the team can respond to a blocker.

sections.title: Blocker communication
sections.text: A blocker should be explained with its effect on testing and the help needed to move forward. Keep the discussion focused on the work and recovery rather than blaming a colleague or listing activity without outcomes.

sections.title: Constructive retrospectives
sections.text: The class discussed what went well, what did not and how to improve communication or availability. In an interview, describe the problem, the improvement suggested and the result honestly; do not present a class example as personal project experience.

sections.title: Automation candidates
sections.text: Repeated, high-volume scenarios can be candidates for automation. Explain the stable workflow and expected outcome first, then discuss how automation could reduce repeated effort while keeping result review.

practice: Prepare a one-minute testing status update.
Turn a process problem into a constructive improvement suggestion.
Describe one repeated check that could be automated and why.

terms.definition: Stand-up: short team coordination around progress and impediments.
Blocker: an impediment that prevents planned work from progressing.
Retrospective: team reflection that identifies practical improvements.
Automation candidate: a repeatable check with a clear purpose and outcome.

review.question: What makes a QA status update useful?
review.answer: It states outcomes, the next work and any impediment needing action.

review.question: How should a blocker be communicated?
review.answer: Explain its impact and the specific support or decision needed.

review.question: What is the purpose of a retrospective?
review.answer: To learn from the iteration and agree practical improvements.

review.question: Which tests may be good automation candidates?
review.answer: Stable, repeated checks with meaningful expected outcomes.

review.question: How should training examples be used in interviews?
review.answer: Use them to explain understanding, while distinguishing training from personal work experience.

sessions.title: Acceptance criteria and ServiceNow end-to-end testing
sessions.summary: This practical session followed a catalog request from its acceptance criteria through requester submission and backend task handling. It also compared incident, problem and change workflows in service management.

sections.title: Environment awareness
sections.text: Identify the environment before interacting with a ServiceNow instance. Confirm that the account and data are approved for testing; development, test, UAT and production have different purposes and access expectations.

sections.title: Acceptance criteria to tests
sections.text: Read the story’s acceptance criteria and turn each observable rule into a check. The lane-closure example included catalog details, required fields and workflow results; ask for clarification when a rule is ambiguous.

sections.title: Requester and backend evidence
sections.text: Follow the portal submission into the generated request item and related tasks. Verify the intended assignment and state changes with approved test roles instead of ending the test at the first confirmation message.

sections.title: Incident, problem and change
sections.text: Incident handling restores service; problem management investigates underlying causes; change management organizes approved modifications. The class used these related workflows to show why a tester must understand the purpose of each record and its transitions.

practice: Break a catalog requirement into field and workflow checks.
Trace one request through its backend records using approved test roles.
Explain the purpose of an incident, a problem and a change record.

terms.definition: Environment: the system instance and configuration in which work runs.
Acceptance criteria: conditions that describe acceptable story behavior.
Request item: the backend record associated with the requested catalog item.
Problem management: investigation and management of underlying incident causes.

review.question: Why identify the environment before testing?
review.answer: To use the correct instance, approved data and permissions.

review.question: How do acceptance criteria guide test design?
review.answer: They describe the observable rules and outcomes that checks must cover.

review.question: Why verify a request item and its tasks?
review.answer: They provide evidence that the submitted request entered and progressed through the workflow.

review.question: How do incident and problem management differ?
review.answer: Incident handling restores service; problem management addresses underlying causes.

review.question: What should happen before a change is implemented?
review.answer: The required approval and workflow conditions should be satisfied.

sessions.title: STLC, defect evidence and requirement traceability
sessions.summary: This interview-preparation session reviewed the sequence from requirement analysis through planning, test execution and defect handling. It emphasized clear test-case evidence, examples of test types and links between requirements and coverage.

sections.title: Planning the testing work
sections.text: The test plan describes what, how and when to test and provides context for execution. Test analysis identifies the appropriate checks, data and risks before individual cases are executed.

sections.title: Action, expected and actual result
sections.text: A useful test case records user actions and expected outcomes; execution adds actual results and status. Keep the observations clear enough that another tester can repeat the check and understand a mismatch.

sections.title: Defect lifecycle
sections.text: When behavior differs from the requirement, record a reproducible defect with evidence. After a fix, verify the original issue and assess related regression risk; reopening and deferred states should reflect the team’s agreed process.

sections.title: Requirement traceability
sections.text: A requirement traceability matrix connects requirements to tests and their coverage. It helps identify missing checks and explain how a requirement was verified; it does not replace the underlying test evidence.

practice: Write one test case and a linked requirement identifier.
Explain a defect’s path from discovery to confirmation of a fix.
Create a small requirement-to-test coverage table.

terms.definition: Test planning: defining the approach, scope and resources for testing.
Actual result: the observed outcome when a test is executed.
Defect lifecycle: the recorded progression of an issue through investigation and resolution.
RTM: a mapping between requirements and their test coverage.

review.question: What does the test plan explain?
review.answer: What will be tested, the approach, timing, resources and relevant criteria.

review.question: When is the actual result recorded?
review.answer: During execution, based on observed behavior.

review.question: What should accompany a defect?
review.answer: Reproduction steps, expected and actual behavior, environment and evidence.

review.question: Why assess regression after a fix?
review.answer: The change may affect related behavior beyond the original defect.

review.question: What question does an RTM help answer?
review.answer: Which tests cover a requirement and where coverage may be missing.

sessions.title: ServiceNow roles, catalog testing and negative checks
sessions.summary: This session introduced ServiceNow interfaces and then followed a catalog-item testing example through story review, requester impersonation, request submission and workflow validation. It also discussed negative date checks and service-level behavior.

sections.title: Environments and roles
sections.text: The session distinguished development, test and UAT contexts and the portal from backend navigation. Confirm the intended environment and role before testing so observations represent the approved workflow.

sections.title: Preparing cases before execution
sections.text: A tester can prepare cases from a story’s acceptance criteria while development is underway. Execution begins when the required readiness conditions are met; the demonstrated board lanes are a team workflow example.

sections.title: Role-based catalog request
sections.text: The demonstration used a requester role for submission and backend views for subsequent checks. Verify the generated records, assignment and closure behavior across the workflow using authorized test roles.

sections.title: Negative tests and SLA scope
sections.text: The class discussed invalid date behavior as a negative-test example and separately introduced SLA checks. Verify that disallowed input is handled correctly, and include SLA behavior when it belongs to the requirement or agreed test scope.

practice: Write a requester-to-backend workflow check from acceptance criteria.
Add an invalid-input case alongside the valid request path.
State explicitly whether SLA behavior is inside or outside your test scope.

terms.definition: UAT: user acceptance testing in the agreed acceptance context.
Ready for testing: a workflow state indicating that a story can proceed to testing.
Requester: the role submitting a service or catalog request.
SLA: a service-level agreement defining relevant service targets.

review.question: Why distinguish portal and backend checks?
review.answer: They expose different stages and evidence of the same request workflow.

review.question: Can case preparation start before development finishes?
review.answer: Yes, when requirements are available; execution still needs readiness.

review.question: Why use authorized test roles for impersonation?
review.answer: To verify the intended permissions and user experience safely.

review.question: What should an invalid-date test prove?
review.answer: That the application handles the invalid date according to the intended rule.

review.question: Should every catalog test include an SLA check?
review.answer: Only when SLA behavior is part of the relevant requirement or agreed scope.

sessions.title: ServiceNow QA workflows, business rules, and interview practice
sessions.summary: This session connects an honest, concise QA introduction with practical ServiceNow testing. It follows a request from the portal into the platform, examines field validation and business rules, and discusses SLA timing, integrations, and regression coverage. Environment-specific examples must be checked against the actual requirement rather than treated as universal ServiceNow behavior.
keyConcepts: SLA pause, resume, and breach checks

sections.title: Describe the QA workflow
sections.text: Describe experience accurately: understand requirements and acceptance criteria, design cases, execute checks, validate workflow and integration behavior, and report defects with evidence. A concise introduction should use genuine experience; the example is a structure to practice rather than a biography to claim.

sections.title: Validate the catalog form
sections.text: Start with the requester role and the correct portal. Compare the catalog item, labels, description, required-field indicators, and valid options with acceptance criteria. Exercise required-field failures and verify the expected feedback. Portal paths and catalog names vary by implementation.

sections.title: Trace requests through roles
sections.text: Record the request identifier after submission, then use the approved fulfiller role in the platform to locate the same request. Check associated requested items, catalog tasks, assignment groups, and approval behavior against the agreed workflow. Refresh state when appropriate and collect reproducible evidence before concluding a defect exists.

sections.title: Check conditional business rules
sections.text: Business rules express required conditional behavior. The class used automatically calculated priority and a cancellation reason as examples. Build a decision table from the actual documented conditions, then test expected outcomes and invalid inputs. The example priority mapping is environment-specific, and the transcript uses emergency where other implementations may use urgency.

sections.title: Test SLA timing in a controlled environment
sections.text: Verify start, pause, resume, and breach behavior against the configured SLA and its business calendar. Shortened test durations require an approved test environment configuration; do not change production timing. The session illustrates excluding paused time, but actual pause conditions, schedules, thresholds, and boundary behavior must come from the SLA definition.

sections.title: Validate connected behavior
sections.text: Trace a request from portal submission to its platform record using stable identifiers. For external API or directory integrations, verify the agreed data mapping and expected downstream result. A portal and platform view may be parts of the same system; call the check end-to-end workflow validation unless a defined integration boundary is being tested.

sections.title: Separate confirmation and regression
sections.text: Rerun a previously failing case to confirm its fix, then check related existing behavior for side effects. The class also discussed missing approval behavior in production. Preserve that specific scenario as a regression check with clear prerequisites and expected results; passing it supplies evidence rather than a guarantee that every future defect is prevented.

practice: Prepare a one-to-two-minute introduction using only experience you can explain and demonstrate.
Write a requester-to-fulfiller test with the request identifier, role changes, expected records, and evidence.
Build a business-rule decision table from documented conditions, including one negative case.
Describe SLA pause/resume and boundary checks without changing production configuration.

terms.definition: Agreed, testable conditions used to judge required behavior.
A record representing an item within a catalog request; verify the configured relationship and workflow.
Conditional behavior defined by business requirements and implemented in the application.
A service-level agreement with configured targets, schedules, and timing conditions.
Repeating a previously failing case to check its specific fix.
Checking whether a change adversely affected existing behavior.

review.question: What should guide expected field and workflow behavior?
review.answer: Validated requirements and acceptance criteria for that implementation.

review.question: Why retain the request identifier after submission?
review.answer: It lets you trace the same request and its related records across views and roles.

review.question: Is the example priority mapping a universal rule?
review.answer: No. Test the mapping documented and configured for the actual environment.

review.question: How can SLA checks run faster safely?
review.answer: Use approved shortened timing in a controlled test environment and verify the real configured rules separately; do not alter production timing.

review.question: How does confirmation testing differ from regression testing?
review.answer: Confirmation checks the specific reported fix; regression checks existing behavior for adverse effects elsewhere.

review.question: What should an interview introduction claim?
review.answer: Only genuine experience and responsibilities that you can explain and support with examples.

sessions.title: UI components, locators, and running Playwright and Cypress examples
sessions.summary: Class Three connects visible UI controls to their HTML attributes and test locators, then walks through selecting a scenario, copying the matching Playwright or Cypress example, saving a test file, and running it in the correct workspace. The session includes hands-on browser-workspace practice and Windows setup troubleshooting. The Windows installation attempt encountered a script-execution restriction; it is not evidence of a successful installation.
keyConcepts: Workspace paths and visible test execution

sections.title: Identify the component and its expected behavior
sections.text: Begin with a small, observable UI behavior: entering text, selecting a dropdown option, checking a checkbox, or choosing a radio option. State the input, action, and expected result before choosing code. A click completing is not enough evidence that the intended result occurred. The practice page supplies small examples so each control can be understood without a large business application.

sections.title: Choose a locator that describes the intended element
sections.text: The class compared locating elements by text, label, placeholder, title, test ID, and markup attributes. A locator identifies the control a test must act on. Inspect the real page and select a locator that distinguishes the intended element. In the Playwright examples, labels and roles connect tests to the interface; the Cypress examples use the practice page’s data-cy attributes.

sections.title: Read tags, attributes, and values
sections.text: Recognize the element tag, its attribute names, and their values when inspecting markup. This explains how a visible field or button relates to a locator. ID and name are examples of attributes, not interchangeable meanings. HTML describes page structure, CSS controls presentation, and the DOM is the browser’s document representation; the class’s HTML/XML analogy should not be interpreted as a rule that XML is the backend.

sections.title: Compare the same text-entry scenario in both frameworks
sections.text: In the demonstrated example, the test enters Ada into the display-name field. The lesson offers Playwright and Cypress versions of the same requirement: compare how each locates the field and enters text, then check the displayed result. Method names differ between frameworks; use the corresponding example rather than mixing calls from the two libraries.

sections.title: Select a scenario and save the matching test file
sections.text: Use the Class Three scenario dropdown, such as minimum-length validation, and select the Playwright or Cypress code tab. The code pane updates for that selection. Copy the complete example into the correct framework’s test file, save it, and check the filename and extension. Preserve completed exercises in separate files when useful so changing one scenario does not erase earlier work.

sections.title: Run from the correct workspace and observe the live browser
sections.text: The hands-on demonstration navigated into the workspace and practice application before running the test. Use cd to change directories; put paths containing spaces inside quotation marks. Keep the editor file, terminal working directory, and selected framework consistent. For hosted practice, open Live test browser to observe a headed run. A successful terminal command is distinct from having the correct browser view open; review the reported test result as well.

sections.title: Follow the Windows setup guide in sequence
sections.text: For desktop practice, download and extract the approved Windows kit, then follow its step-by-step guide. Setup is separate from running a test; the class navigated into the extracted folder and attempted Setup.cmd. The recording shows troubleshooting and an execution-policy/signature error, not a completed installation. Use the current published guide and verified package; report errors rather than disabling system-wide execution policy or assuming the tools installed.

sections.title: Use repeatable checks for regression coverage
sections.text: The discussion connected automation to regression: rerun meaningful checks of existing behavior after changes. Understand the requirement and expected result first, then automate a stable example. Keep evidence of what ran and what passed or failed. A template is a starting point; adapt locators, inputs, and assertions to the application being tested instead of treating copied code as proof of coverage.

practice: Choose the text-entry scenario. Run the Playwright example and explain its locator, action, and result assertion.
Run the matching Cypress example in its separate framework file; compare its data-cy locator and typing command with Playwright.
Select minimum-length validation. State the invalid input and expected blocked-save behavior before running the test.
Save each exercise with the correct filename and extension; identify the terminal’s current directory before execution.
Open the hosted Live test browser when observing a headed test, then record the scenario, framework, outcome, and any error.
For desktop setup, use the current Windows guide in order and preserve the exact installer error if a prerequisite check fails.

terms.definition: A visible interactive part of a page, such as a text field, dropdown, checkbox, or button.
A named property in an element’s markup, such as id, name, or a dedicated data-cy value.
A description used by a test framework to identify a particular page element.
A check that observed behavior matches the expected outcome.
The folder relative paths and commands currently operate from.
Checking existing behavior for unwanted effects after a change.

review.question: What should you define before copying a component test?
review.answer: The scenario’s input, action, and observable expected result.

review.question: What connects a visible control to a test action?
review.answer: A locator that identifies the intended element using the real page’s semantics or attributes.

review.question: Can Playwright and Cypress method names be mixed in one example?
review.answer: No. Use the complete example for the selected framework and its own test runner.

review.question: Why save the test in the correct framework folder?
review.answer: The runner must discover the appropriate file and execute it with the intended configuration.

review.question: Why does cd matter when running a test?
review.answer: It sets the working directory used by commands and relative file paths; quoted paths handle spaces.

review.question: Where should a student observe a hosted headed run?
review.answer: In the assigned workspace’s Live test browser, while also checking the terminal’s test outcome.

review.question: Did the Windows troubleshooting in this recording prove setup succeeded?
review.answer: No. A script-execution error was encountered; successful setup requires passing the current package’s checks.

review.question: Does copying a template prove a requirement is covered?
review.answer: No. Verify that its locators, data, actions, and assertions match the requirement, then execute and inspect the result.

sessions.title: Class Two lab — workspace access and visible Playwright execution
sessions.summary: The October 7 lab continues Class Two with hands-on workspace practice. Students connect the editor, terminal, practice application and test browser, and distinguish running a command from observing the expected UI behavior. These focused notes cover the verified lab passages; lengthy access and deployment troubleshooting is condensed. Class 2.1 is this library’s supplemental-session identifier, not a new lecture number announced in the recording.

sections.title: Start in the assigned workspace
sections.text: The instructor introduces the shared workspace as the place for supervised practice. Open the assigned environment and locate the practice project before running an exercise. Workspace access and the practice website serve different purposes: the workspace provides files and a terminal, while the application is what the test exercises. The recording describes a historical setup; check the current classroom instructions for today’s access status.

sections.title: Plan the shared practice session
sections.text: The lab describes a two-hour daily allocation and one student using the shared practice resource at a time. Prepare the scenario and files before starting so session time goes toward execution and investigation. Save the work before ending the session. This discussion is not proof of simultaneous capacity or a guarantee that an old account or service is currently available.

sections.title: Turn a use case into a small hands-on check
sections.text: The purpose of this session is to apply the earlier UI concepts through the Academy’s practice cases. Select one behavior, identify the input and action, and state what should change on the page. Run the corresponding example and compare its assertion with that expected outcome. Hosted and desktop practice are alternative environments; use the current guide for the one you are working in.

sections.title: Keep the lab connected to Class Two
sections.text: The instructor explicitly identifies the session as a Class Two lab and brings the whiteboard back into the teaching flow. Revisit the earlier class materials when a locator, control or assertion is unfamiliar. Keep a short lab record with the scenario, framework, expected outcome, observed outcome and any error so repeating a test also reinforces the concept.

sections.title: Inspect the command before changing settings
sections.text: During the visible-browser investigation, the instructor asks to see the command again. Check what was actually executed: the selected test, framework, working directory and flags. Compare the command with the current class guide. A test process starting, a browser window opening, and an assertion passing are separate observations; record each instead of assuming one proves the others.

sections.title: Separate a test run from its visible browser view
sections.text: A participant reports that no new browser window appeared. In a hosted environment, the browser runs within the workspace environment and its live view must be opened through the provided classroom route. A headed option alone does not prove the view is connected. Preserve the terminal result and report the visible symptom; the troubleshooting in this recording should not be treated as a current deployment health check.

sections.title: Use the editor’s terminal deliberately
sections.text: The lab returns to the editor and its terminal while investigating execution. The editor holds the saved test; the terminal runs the project’s commands. Verify the current directory and save the file before rerunning. Use the published command for the selected framework and retain the complete error message when asking for help, while keeping account credentials out of shared screenshots.

practice: Choose one Class Two scenario and write its input, action and expected result before running it.
Locate the saved test file and identify the terminal’s current directory.
Execute the current guide’s test command and record the actual test outcome.
For a hosted headed run, open Live test browser and confirm that the view shows the same exercise.
Save the test and a short outcome/error record before stopping the session.

terms.definition: The environment containing the editor, project files and terminal used for practice.
The folder from which a terminal command resolves relative project paths.
A test run that uses a browser with a graphical display in its execution environment.
A check that the observed result matches the required behavior.

review.question: What is the difference between the workspace and the practice application?
review.answer: The workspace provides the editor, files and terminal; the application is the system the test exercises.

review.question: What should you decide before executing an example?
review.answer: The scenario’s input, action and observable expected result.

review.question: Does a started command prove that the expected UI behavior passed?
review.answer: No. Read the runner result and inspect the relevant assertion and application behavior.

review.question: Does a headed option alone prove that the hosted live view is connected?
review.answer: No. Open the provided live-browser route and verify that it shows the intended run.

review.question: What should you inspect before changing configuration?
review.answer: The actual command, selected framework and test, saved file, working directory and reported error.

review.question: Why keep a short lab record?
review.answer: It connects the expected outcome with the observed result and makes reruns and troubleshooting reproducible.

sessions.title: ServiceNow testing — request lifecycle, approvals, access and notifications
sessions.summary: The October 14 first interview-preparation session rehearses an end-to-end ServiceNow testing explanation, using salary and cloud-request catalog examples. It links portal fields to requests, requested items, catalog tasks, approvals and closure, then extends the discussion to access changes, notifications and configuration items. Every expected state, approval and assignment group must come from the project’s acceptance criteria; the demonstrated workflow is not a universal ServiceNow configuration.
keyConcepts: Acceptance criteria as the test oracle
Request, requested item and catalog task

sections.title: Determine approval requirements from the story
sections.text: Check the story’s acceptance criteria before using the Approval tab as evidence. The instructor describes both possible defects: an unwanted approval added to a no-approval flow, and a required approval omitted from the implementation. For each catalog item, test the specified approval path and its expected approver; do not infer correctness simply because the UI contains or lacks a tab.

sections.title: Validate the portal catalog item before submission
sections.text: In the salary example, locate the catalog item as the permitted test requester. Compare the item name and description, field labels, field types, required indicators and available choices with the acceptance criteria. In the cloud-request example, the request type and multi-line business justification have specific requirements. Include missing required input and invalid choices when the story defines their handling.

sections.title: Trace the same request through the backend
sections.text: Record the identifier returned after portal submission, then use the authorized fulfiller perspective to locate the same business request. Distinguish the request from its requested item (RITM) and the service catalog task. Confirm the required records and relationships were generated. The transcript sometimes renders RITM as “return”; these notes use the ServiceNow term requested item rather than interpreting that transcription literally.

sections.title: Validate assignment and closure transitions
sections.text: Check the catalog task’s assignment group against the story, then complete the task using the state required by the example. Revisit the requested item and refresh to observe its resulting state. In this demonstrated configuration, task completion should close the requested item. In another project, additional tasks, approvals or flow conditions may alter that outcome; the acceptance criteria define the expected transition.

sections.title: Turn each acceptance criterion into test evidence
sections.text: The cloud-request walkthrough identifies the business-justification description as a required multi-line field. Write a step and expected result for each relevant criterion, including label, type, required behavior and choice values. Record the actual result rather than describing only the clicks. A submitted form does not by itself prove that all field requirements were met.

sections.title: Validate access removal as well as access grants
sections.text: For the access-request example, follow the configured request and approval process using authorized test identities. Confirm that a granted user appears in the expected group, or that a removed user is absent. Where the story requires effective access testing, impersonate the permitted test user and verify the protected function is allowed or denied as specified. Group membership is evidence about provisioning; it is not a complete test of every ACL rule.

sections.title: Verify notification identity and content
sections.text: Find the relevant ServiceNow email record for the event under test and compare the expected subject, sender, recipient and message body. Tie its confirmation or request identifier back to the same request. An email record in the platform and receipt in an external mailbox are different observations. Check actual external receipt only when it is required and an approved test mailbox is available.

sections.title: Keep notification tests within authorized test data
sections.text: The instructor explains that whether testers may use an external mailbox depends on the project’s allowed procedure. Use the supplied test identity and approved mailbox; do not substitute a personal address without permission. State clearly whether the test verified the ServiceNow notification record, external receipt, or both so the evidence does not overstate delivery.

sections.title: Validate CMDB information within the assigned scope
sections.text: CMDB stores information about configuration items, such as applications and infrastructure. In the class’s dashboard example, verify that the expected widgets and CI details appear for the permitted role and match the story. Where CI records are part of the test, check the specified attributes and relationships. UI or record validation does not establish deep database administration expertise, and these notes do not claim every demonstrated environment had all features configured.

practice: Write positive and negative checks for the cloud request’s required request type and business justification fields.
Trace a sample submission through request, RITM and catalog task, recording each identifier and relationship.
Compare one required-approval scenario and one no-approval scenario against the story.
Verify a configured assignment group and the resulting requested-item state after task completion.
Describe both membership and effective-permission checks for an access-removal requirement.
Prepare a notification evidence table separating platform content checks from approved mailbox receipt.
Rehearse an interview answer using context, your actual role, test actions, expected results and evidence; do not claim the classroom example as employment experience.

terms.definition: The authoritative expected behavior used to judge a result; here, the approved acceptance criteria.
A requested item record associated with a service request.
A task used to fulfill work for a requested item in the configured workflow.
Using an authorized test identity’s perspective to validate its permitted behavior.
An access-control rule governing permitted operations on protected resources; testing may require more than checking group membership.
The configuration management database and the configuration items whose attributes and relationships it records.

review.question: Why compare the story with the Approval tab?
review.answer: The implementation may add an unnecessary approval or omit a required one. The story defines what should happen.

review.question: Which records should you distinguish after a catalog submission?
review.answer: The request, its requested item (RITM), and the required catalog task records and their relationships.

review.question: What should a portal field check include?
review.answer: The specified label, description, field type, required behavior, available choices and expected validation.

review.question: Does completing any catalog task always close its RITM?
review.answer: No. That is the demonstrated scenario’s expected outcome; other configurations may require more tasks or conditions.

review.question: Is a group-membership check a complete ACL test?
review.answer: No. Check membership provisioning and, where required, the test user’s effective permission on the protected operation.

review.question: Does a ServiceNow email record prove mailbox receipt?
review.answer: No. Platform notification content and external mailbox delivery need separate evidence.

review.question: When can an external email address be used?
review.answer: Only under the project’s approved test procedure with an authorized test mailbox.

review.question: What is appropriate CMDB evidence for the dashboard example?
review.answer: The expected role can view the required widgets and CI details, and the specified fields match the acceptance criteria.

sessions.title: Second interview session — partial recording; teaching transcript unavailable
sessions.summary: This entry preserves the October 14 second-session recording, which is a 16-minute 15-second segment. The available WebEx transcript contains only 21 brief greetings and fragmented lines, and its recap reports no substantive teaching discussion. There is not enough reliable material to generate lesson notes or review answers for this segment. Use the first session’s ServiceNow notes for study; they are a separate source, not a reconstructed transcript of this recording.
